newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler to invest $1.2 billion in Ohio Jeep plant.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler to invest $1.2 billion in Ohio Jeep plant.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. said Monday it will invest $1.2 billion in a new Jeep assembly plant and existing facilities in Toledo, Ohio, ending months of speculation about the future of Jeep production there.
Under a deal struck with state and local officials, Chrysler said it will build a new, 1.1 million-square-foot assembly plant adjacent to its existing Stickney Avenue plant on Toledo's north side.
Construction of the $600 million plant is scheduled to start in 1998, with assembly of Jeep Cherokee and Wrangler sport utility vehicles starting there in 2001.
Chrysler will spend another $600 million to refurbish an existing 290,000-square-foot building on the Stickney site and make other improvements to its nearby Jeep Parkway plant.
The investment ensures the future of the sprawling Toledo Jeep complex, the city's largest employer, which has built Jeeps since the sturdy vehicle's inception during World War II.

Parts of the current factories were first built in 1910, making them among the oldest operating auto plants in the world. They went through several owners before Chrysler acquired them in its 1987 buyout of American Motors Corp.

Chrysler said last year it would replace the creaking factories with a new state-of-the-art plant located somewhere in the Toledo area, but with Monday's announcement, it committed to its existing inner-city "brownfield" location.
In 1991, Chrysler built a new Jeep plant near downtown Detroit across the street from its old Jefferson Avenue plant, keeping the same work force.
But the new, refurbished Toledo plants will operate with fewer workers -- employment is expected to drop to 4,900 people from about 5,400 currently through retirements and normal attrition.

"Our major consideration was to have a new manufacturing facility that would allow us to retain our current outstanding Toledo work force, and capitalise on their continuous commitment to building world-class products," Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton said in a statement.
"The entire corporation was touched by the outpouring of support displayed by the people of Toledo,"

The state of Ohio committed an incentive package worth $127 million to the project, including a $96.6 million investment tax credit, environmental cleanup grandts and credits and assistance for land acquisition and infrastructure costs.

The project will reconfigure the plants' production system. Currently, the Parkway plant assembles the four-door Cherokees and builds the two-door Wrangler bodies, which are then shipped to the Stickney plant for final assembly.

When the improvements are complete, the expanded Stickney plant will become the main final assembly facility for both Cherokees and Wranglers. The Parkway plant, which will get an upgraded paint shop and other improvements, will continue to build and ship Wrangler bodies to the Stickney plant.
